title: Cap. III Rat. 3: king’s prize — no glory-decree before victory / perseverance foresight
latin: Rat. 3. In Divina voluntate ordo actuum consideratur non per se, sed ex analogia quadam ad voluntatem humanam: unde secundum nostrum intelligendi modum aliquid prius, aliquid posterius a Deo volitum sive praevisum affirmamus. Hoc posito contendit Vasques, Sicuti cum Rex aliquis proponit premium bene certantibus, ea lege ut nullus illo potiatur nisi qui victor sit, nunquam decernit alicui, quantumvis amato, dare illud premium, antequam illum videat victoria potitum; ita de Deo sentiendum, nunquam illum decernere alicui premium aeternae gloriae, quod tanquam coronam promisit legitime certantibus, nisi post intuitum victoriae, hoc est, perseverantiae in bonis operibus. Jam vero quia Deus est praescius omnium futurorum, ab aeterno praevidit quinam victoriam reportabunt, atque idcirco ab aeterno ex hac praevisione decrevit illis dare gloriam: sicuti princeps, cum videt aliquem vicisse, tum demum statuit illi premium assignare.
pass_a: Reason 3. In the divine will the order of acts is considered not in itself, but from a certain analogy to the human will: whence according to our mode of understanding we affirm something earlier, something later as willed or foreseen by God. This having been posited, Vasquez contends: Just as when some king proposes a prize to those contending well, by that law that no one obtain it unless he be victor, he never decrees to anyone, however beloved, to give that prize before he sees him possessed of the victory; so it must be thought of God, that he never decrees to anyone the prize of eternal glory, which he promised as a crown to those contending lawfully, except after the intuition of victory, that is, of perseverance in good works. But now because God is foreknower of all futures, from eternity he foresaw who would carry off the victory, and therefore from eternity from this foresight he decreed to give them glory: just as a prince, when he sees someone has conquered, then at last decides to assign him the prize.
pass_b: Rat. 3. In God’s will the order of acts is not read in itself but by analogy to human willing — so in our way of speaking we call one thing prior and another later as willed or foreseen by God. On that footing Vasquez presses: as a king who sets a prize for those who contend well, on the rule that only the victor takes it, never decrees to give that prize to anyone — however loved — before he sees him possessed of the victory, so of God: he never decrees to anyone the prize of eternal glory (promised as a crown to those who contend lawfully) except after intuition of victory, that is perseverance in good works. And since God foreknows all futures, from eternity he foresaw who would win, and from that foresight decreed to give them glory — as a prince, seeing someone has conquered, only then resolves to assign the prize.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3: grant analogy-order; God can destine the crown from mere grace first
latin: Sol. Concedimus illud postulatum, nimirum, Non esse aliquem ordinem prioritatis & posterioritatis in actibus sive voluntatis sive mentis Divinae; sed hunc ordinem desumi ex analogia ad voluntatem humanam; & ex dependentia obiectorum, quam habent inter se. Ad inductam autem comparationem respondemus, Primo, posse nos manifestam causam afferre cur Princeps terrestris non designat aliquem singulariter ad premium, nisi ex precedente intuitu Victoriae, & Deus tamen possit e contra primo ex mera gratia destinare aliquem singulariter ad coronam, & consequenter praeparate & dare illi ea dona, per quae praevidebitur producendus ad coronam.
pass_a: Solution. We grant that postulate, namely, that there is not any order of priority and posteriority in the acts either of the divine will or of the divine mind; but that this order is taken from analogy to the human will; and from the dependence of objects which they have among themselves. But to the comparison brought in we answer, First, that we can bring a manifest cause why an earthly prince does not designate someone singularly to the prize except from a preceding intuition of Victory, and yet God on the contrary can first from mere grace destine someone singularly to the crown, and consequently prepare and give him those gifts through which he will be foreseen as one to be brought forth to the crown.
pass_b: Sol. We grant the postulate: there is no priority/posteriority in the acts of the divine will or mind themselves; that order is borrowed from analogy to human willing and from how the objects depend on one another. To the comparison itself: first, we can show why an earthly prince does not mark someone out for the prize except after seeing the victory — and yet God, on the contrary, can first from mere grace destine someone singularly to the crown, and then prepare and give the gifts through which that person will be foreseen as brought to the crown.

lemmas.lemma: non esse ordinem prioritatis in actibus Divinae
ex mera gratia destinare ad coronam

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3: mortal king cannot inspire victory-powers — if he could, not from foresight
latin: Ratio autem haec est; Quia non est penes Regem mortalem inspirare & infundere illam voluntatem, & illas vires ex quibus infallibiliter haec singularis persona prae aliis obtineat victoriam. Si hoc posset, nihil impediret, quin cuicunque amico suo ex primaria & gratuita voluntate intenderet & decerneret dare illud premium, ita tamen ut perveniret ad illud secundum legem positam, nimirum vincendo, idque ex viribus illi inspiratis virtute primariae illius intentionis. Si ita res se haberet in terreno Principe, non ex praevisione meritorum elegisse diceretur amicum suum ad premium obtinendum, sed ex antecedente proposito & intentione dandi premium, dedisse merita, & in hac sua donatione praevidisse. At sic agere Deum cum omnibus glorificandis in confesso est.
pass_a: But the reason is this: Because it is not in the power of a mortal king to inspire and infuse that will, and those powers, from which infallibly this singular person rather than others obtains the victory. If he could do this, nothing would hinder but that to whichever friend of his he might from a primary and gratuitous will intend and decree to give that prize, yet so that he should arrive at it according to the law laid down, namely by conquering, and that from powers inspired into him by virtue of that primary intention. If the matter so stood in an earthly Prince, he would not be said to have elected his friend to obtaining the prize from foresight of merits, but from an antecedent purpose and intention of giving the prize, to have given the merits, and in this his donation to have foreseen. But that God so acts with all who are to be glorified is confessed.
pass_b: The reason: a mortal king cannot inspire and pour in the will and powers by which this one person rather than others infallibly wins. If he could, nothing would stop him intending and decreeing from a primary, gratuitous will to give that prize to any friend — yet so the friend reaches it by the stated law, namely by winning, and from powers inspired by that primary intention. Were an earthly prince so able, we would not say he elected his friend to the prize from foresight of merits, but that from an antecedent purpose to give the prize he gave the merits and in that gift foresaw them. And that God so deals with all who are to be glorified is confessed.

lemmas.lemma: non est penes Regem mortalem inspirare

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3: efficacious end-intention before victory; God more than agonothetes
latin: Secundo, quod assumit Vasques, non posse Principem intendere efficaciter ut aliquis consequatur premium, nisi ex praeviso intuitu meritorum, non est tam exploratae veritatis, atque ille opinatur. Est enim efficax intentio finis, quae movet agentem ut efficaciter adhibeat quaecunque potest media ad eiusdem consecutionem: licet non sit in eius potestate certo praevidere eventum, aut infallibiliter ipsum finem consequi. Potest igitur Princeps ex speciali benevolentia serio & efficaciter intendere praemium amico suo ante intuitum victoriae; atque ex hac intentione non modo optare, sed quantum in illo est, parare & dare illi omnia quae conducunt ad victoriam; quamvis ut judex & agonothetes non possit illum actu coronare, nisi intuitu victoriae obtentae. Deus ergo multo magis (cui velle & facere aeque in promptu sunt) potest efficaciter intendere Petro aut Paulo coronam aeternae gloriae, atque ex vi hujus intentionis praeparate & dare illis ea omnia quae merita coronae dicuntur; atque in hac sua praedestinatione ab aeterno praevidere illorum merita, atque tandem intuitu pugnae praeclare depugnatae coronam destinatam illorum capitibus imponere.
pass_a: Second, what Vasquez assumes, that a Prince cannot efficaciously intend that someone obtain the prize except from a foreseen intuition of merits, is not of so explored a truth as he opines. For there is an efficacious intention of the end which moves the agent to apply efficaciously whatsoever means he can to the obtaining of the same: although it be not in his power certainly to foresee the event, or infallibly to obtain the end itself. A Prince therefore from special benevolence can seriously and efficaciously intend the prize for his friend before the intuition of victory; and from this intention not only wish, but as far as in him is, prepare and give him all things that conduce to victory; although as judge and agonothetes he cannot actually crown him except upon intuition of the victory obtained. God therefore much more (for whom to will and to do are equally at hand) can efficaciously intend for Peter or Paul the crown of eternal glory, and from the force of this intention prepare and give them all those things which are called merits of the crown; and in this his predestination from eternity foresee their merits, and at length upon intuition of the fight nobly fought place the destined crown upon their heads.
pass_b: Second, Vasquez’s claim that a prince cannot efficaciously intend someone’s prize except from foresight of merits is not as settled as he thinks. Efficacious intention of an end moves the agent to apply every means in his power toward obtaining it — even when he cannot certainly foresee the event or infallibly secure the end. So a prince from special goodwill can seriously and efficaciously intend the prize for his friend before seeing the victory, and from that intention not only wish but, as far as he can, prepare and give all that helps toward victory — though as judge and agonothetes he cannot actually crown him except upon the victory won. God much more (for whom to will and to do are ready alike) can efficaciously intend for Peter or Paul the crown of eternal glory, and by that intention’s force prepare and give all that are called merits of the crown; and in this predestination from eternity foresee their merits, and at last, upon the fight nobly fought, set the destined crown on their heads.

title: Cap. III Sol. Rat. 3 close: Augustine — gratuitous election before merits; Hypognost. 6
latin: Postremo, dicimus hanc esse ipsissimam sententiam quam Augustinus passim propugnat contra Pelagianos, nimirum, Eligi homines gratuito, & ante omnem praescientiam meritorum, non modo ad dona gratiae, sed etiam ad regnum gloriae: utcunque perducantur ad regnum gloriae per viam bonorum operum, sive meritorum, ut loqui solent antiqui Patres. Unicum tantummodo locum citabo, qui sic se habet, De damnabili humani generis massa Deus praescivit misericordia, non meritis, quos ex electione gratiae praedestinavit ad vitam, Contra Pelag. Hypognost. lib. 6. Ubi videtis praescientiam illam, qua nititur praedestinatio ad vitam, non esse meritorum nostrorum, sed misericordiae Divinae, qui decrevit nos eligere ex massa damnabili ad participationem vitae aeternae, atque meritis ornare.
pass_a: Finally, we say that this is the very sentence which Augustine everywhere defends against the Pelagians, namely, That men are elected gratuitously, and before all foresight of merits, not only to the gifts of grace, but also to the kingdom of glory: however they be brought to the kingdom of glory by the way of good works, or of merits, as the ancient Fathers are wont to speak. I will cite only one place, which stands thus: From the damnable mass of the human race God foresaw by mercy, not by merits, those whom by election of grace he predestined to life, Contra Pelagianos Hypognosticon book 6. Where you see that that foresight on which predestination to life rests is not of our merits, but of the divine mercy, who decreed to elect us from the damnable mass to participation of eternal life, and to adorn us with merits.
pass_b: Finally, this is the very sentence Augustine everywhere defends against the Pelagians: men are elected gratuitously and before all foresight of merits — not only to gifts of grace but also to the kingdom of glory — however they are brought there by the path of good works or merits, as the ancient Fathers usually speak. One place only: From the damnable mass of the human race God foresaw by mercy, not merits, those whom by election of grace he predestined to life (Contra Pelag. Hypognost. 6). So the foresight on which predestination to life rests is not of our merits but of divine mercy, who decreed to elect us from that damnable mass to share eternal life and to adorn us with merits.

lemmas.lemma: Eligi homines gratuito ante praescientiam meritorum
